#6084. A Less-Is-More Strategy for America

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

BARRY R. POSEN is Ford International Professor of Political Science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

The Folly of Expanding the Exhausted U.S. Military

On October 8, the USS Abraham Lincoln and its accompanying strike group returned to the United States after 320 days at sea. The deployment—a near record for the modern American military—had become controversial. As the group’s ships went month after month without a port call, conditions deteriorated precipitously. Sailors reported supply shortages, plumbing issues, and water contamination. Morale dropped markedly; eight sailors even tried to commit suicide. By the time the ships finally left the Middle East, their struggles had made headlines across the country.

The travails of the Lincoln are hardly the only story about the U.S. military to generate alarm since the war in Iran began last February. Military analysts have expressed concern about other carrier groups’ lengthy deployments. They have fretted about the Trump administration’s decision to pull soldiers and weapons stationed in the Indo-Pacific out of the region and position them in the Middle East. Perhaps most of all, they have worried as the United States drains its stockpile of sophisticated munitions.

These problems all share the same root cause: the U.S. military is not built for the near-constant use it has experienced for decades. Ever since the Cold War, American defense planners have structured the U.S. armed forces to be ready to fight two major conflicts simultaneously. In practice, that means Washington has constructed a force that is designed to win short, sharp wars. For that reason, the military does not have enough units, weapons, or personnel to handle never-ending conflicts and simultaneously use its forces around the world to coerce enemies and reassure partners.

American officials are now trying to modestly increase the size of the military. More important, they are hoping that huge infusions of money will increase the capability of the existing armed forces. But making these changes will be exceptionally challenging—and they are unnecessary. The United States is a highly secure country with many capable and wealthy partners. It does not need a defense apparatus capable of fighting everywhere all at once. Instead, it would be much better off focusing its attention on a smaller set of issues and scaling down accordingly.

The U.S. nonnuclear forces, which consume more than 80 percent of the defense budget, are structured and sized for particular contingencies—currently, a clash with China, Russia, or both nearly simultaneously. The military’s weapons are therefore designed for maximum lethality and survivability in what military planners expect to be an unbelievably dangerous environment. To that end, the Pentagon has emphasized purchasing precise, long-range, and stealthy weapons. These are supposed to kick open the doors of enemy defenses and allow other expensive advanced platforms, such as F-35 fighter jets or B-2 or B-21 bombers, to deliver large quantities of slightly less sophisticated but still quite lethal precision weapons.

Washington has never expected these wars to last long. Instead, it imagines that under the fierce pressure such conflicts would generate, the adversary will cry uncle or the war will escalate to nuclear threats or—worse yet—nuclear use. During the Cold War, for example, the United States and its allies planned for an extremely intense, roughly 30-day conflict against the Soviet Union. Today’s military planners have probably made similar assumptions about a war with Beijing or Moscow. Highly capable conventional forces and the risk of nuclear escalation, American thinking goes, should deter an attack. If deterrence fails, U.S. planners hope to stop an enemy in its tracks and create escalation risks so great that the adversary will realize its errors and try to reverse course.

But such thinking means that Washington does not have enough resources to sustain long, great-power conflicts. At $100 million each, the F-35 fighter aircraft, a mainstay of the air force, navy, and Marine Corps, is simply not designed for mass production. Neither are the long-range stand-off missiles that would be the preferred munitions in the early days of such a war. The U.S. military has developed sophisticated theater ballistic missile defenses, but their main purpose is to defend U.S. forces and essential military infrastructure—not towns, cities, and civilian industries. They can be used for this purpose under certain conditions, but doing so quickly exhausts the supply of missiles. In a war with China or Russia, civilians in local, allied countries will need to look after themselves.

These problems have become readily apparent in Washington’s war against Iran. The United States likely thought it could rapidly overpower the Islamic Republic—at best a middle power, albeit one with great ambitions. After all, under the right circumstances, the U.S. military handily overmatches these kinds of enemies, as it did Iraq in the 1990–91 Gulf War. But Washington’s enemies have smartened up since then. They no longer simply produce smaller and less capable versions of the great-power militaries that American forces are designed to deter and combat. Instead, they have prepared themselves to take a beating and keep on fighting, even if at modest levels of effectiveness.

Overly ambitious war plans and faulty policies are not the only reason the U.S. military is struggling. Politics is also creating difficulties. Because the American people hesitate to support wars abroad, U.S. politicians will do anything to avoid casualties. That means they take all the high-end weaponry that the military stockpiles to break down great-power defenses and instead spend it profligately on regional conflicts. Similarly, they deploy scarce air defense weapons to protect allies’ towns and cities, lest those allies consider finding new partners or decide to settle a war by compromising with their enemies.

U.S. policymakers also generally overuse the military. Politicians like to accompany diplomatic messaging with action, in part because they do not believe in diplomacy anymore, which pushes them to parade or use the armed forces far more often than is warranted. When asked to act, commanders usually salute and say yes. Others simply cannot sit still. Commanders, after all, took on their roles because they wanted to command something.

The result is a worn-down military. The defense press is full of stories about ships and aircraft that are not up to standard because they have been out too long, resulting in deferred maintenance. This, in turn, creates repair problems for other units. When a ship must stay in dry dock longer than usual to receive adequate repairs, other ships must wait longer for servicing—which means their needs also grow. Ultimately, the navy has fewer fully ready combat ships available in the event of a great-power challenge. The army has similar problems, with combat and support vehicles arriving at maintenance depots in unexpectedly poor condition. In the air force, the F-35’s “full mission capable rate,” which was never great, has deteriorated from 38 percent to 25 percent since 2021. And the overall readiness of air force aircraft has declined in recent years, in part simply because of overwork.

All the while, U.S. soldiers, sailors, pilots, and marines are constantly on guard, coercing and deterring U.S. enemies and reassuring allies. This, too, creates high levels of activity that can negatively affect retention. Although the military has generally been successful at retaining senior enlisted personnel in recent years, it may soon run into difficulty. Since 2024, navy warships have repeatedly gone to sea undercrewed. The ultimate result of this overuse is that the sharp edge of the military is dulled, and the steel blade is weakened.

U.S. defense officials are aware that they have a problem. Currently, they are trying to solve it by building a somewhat bigger and far more technologically capable military. Congress, for example, appears poised to increase the Pentagon’s so-called base budget—which encompasses what the Congressional Budget Office defines as the “enduring costs of manning, training, and equipping the military”—by over 25 percent, or to $1.1 trillion for the 2027 fiscal year. The Pentagon hopes to secure an additional $350 billion over the base budget in a subsequent bill. Defense officials also want to add over 40,000 new service members. But this is, at best, a personnel increase of three percent, which is much too small to fill the additional units needed to solve extant readiness problems. And the fancier weapons Congress hopes defense officials will buy cannot overcome the strain of constant deployments and repeated wars. The defense industrial base is barely keeping up with current demands, and recruiting large numbers of new service members would likely require offering much higher wages, which would then need to be extended to everyone else. Personnel costs would start consuming an ever-greater share of the defense budget. U.S. officials could instead opt for conscription, but that would produce a backlash.

There is, however, an alternative: scaling down. Instead of pretending that it must be able to fight two great-power wars at once, Washington should cut its policy coat to fit the available cloth. It should continue to build forces for major contingencies, such as deterring adventurism by China. But policymakers should agree to slow down other projects. Congress should task the Pentagon with reviewing the armed forces and come up with an activity budget, which would be based on an assessment of how much real military activity—flying hours, ship days at sea, training days in the field—can be undertaken without harming the readiness of the total force. It would then allocate that activity appropriately. Based on what they ought to know about the virtual attrition the military has suffered thanks to 30 years of hyperactivity, commanders should determine what level of exercises, forward deployments, and regional wars the military can actually support without doing damage to the capabilities it wishes to have ready every day to deter a great-power war and, if need be, wage one effectively. The U.S. Navy already knows the activity level that its fleet can support, which it has detailed in its Optimized Fleet Response Plan. But American presidents and defense secretaries have simply ignored this plan whenever they wanted to deploy more forces.

The activity budget should not be classified but instead should be public information, listed along with the dollar budget that the Pentagon publishes annually, voluminous summaries of which can be found at the Defense Department’s comptroller’s website. When politicians want to exceed the activity levels on which they have previously agreed, they should have to explain why and how they plan to repair the force after intense use. Commanders should think of this as an ethical issue. Every now and then, one should resign when overuse causes serious problems.

To help lighten its load, Washington will need to hand off some responsibilities to others. This should be feasible despite the need to manage Moscow’s aggressive impulses, which are the presumed cause of one of the contingencies—a war with Russia—that drives U.S. defense planning. The principal European states have more than enough economic and technological resources to deal with Russia on their own, if they so choose. The transatlantic bargain should thus be more forthright about the limited liability that the United States is prepared to assume for the continent’s defense.

The National Defense Strategy of the Trump administration is honest about this fact, but U.S. military activity levels and deployments in Europe suggest that the United States has not truly reduced its role in Europe’s defense. The supreme allied commander of NATO is still an American, when the position should be filled by a European. Tens of thousands of U.S. troops are still based all over Europe; many should come home. Pentagon websites and those of American commands in Europe feature laundry lists of exercises and maneuvers across the continent that involve not only forward-based U.S. forces but also rotating deployments of units based in the United States. These numbers, too, should diminish.

American officials may want to be able to solve most of their global security challenges by simply buying more forces. But a much better solution is for the United States to change its grand strategy and act with greater restraint. Washington simply does not have the will or the resources to provide for both Asia’s and Europe’s defense while fighting protracted conflicts elsewhere, most recently in the Middle East. Nor, for that matter, does it need to. The United States is inherently a very secure country. It is rich, endowed with bountiful natural resources, insulated by vast oceans, and blessed with relatively weak and pliant neighbors. Only huge changes in the political constellation of power in Asia, Europe, or the greater Middle East could seriously affect U.S. security.

Washington should buy sufficient military power and stock adequate reserves of raw materials to ensure against such changes. But in general, it can afford to be less proactive. A change in grand strategy might even allow the United States to cut the defense budget. If concerns about the ballooning U.S. deficits are correct, then the Pentagon will need to help pay the bills to set things right.

Analysis: Iran Is Talking Peace but Preparing for War

Last week, a high-ranking set of Saudi, Pakistani, and Turkish officials came to Tehran, where they met an Iranian delegation led by Mohsen Rezaei. Rezaei, former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), heads Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC). The SNSC is the country’s top decision-making body and brings together leaders from the IRGC and conventional military, along with representatives of the supreme leader and elected officials. In this meeting, Rezaei was joined by President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

That these officials—representing Iran’s top security body, its president, and its foreign minister—all participated in the meeting suggests a degree of consensus across Iran’s political spectrum. In the past, many Iranian diplomatic efforts had been the sole prerogative of the foreign ministry, without buy-in from military and security institutions, which made their implementation difficult. This meeting, on the other hand, demonstrates that, across different centers of power, Iran’s political and military establishment is serious about diplomacy.

Last week, a high-ranking set of Saudi, Pakistani, and Turkish officials came to Tehran, where they met an Iranian delegation led by Mohsen Rezaei. Rezaei, former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), heads Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC). The SNSC is the country’s top decision-making body and brings together leaders from the IRGC and conventional military, along with representatives of the supreme leader and elected officials. In this meeting, Rezaei was joined by President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

That these officials—representing Iran’s top security body, its president, and its foreign minister—all participated in the meeting suggests a degree of consensus across Iran’s political spectrum. In the past, many Iranian diplomatic efforts had been the sole prerogative of the foreign ministry, without buy-in from military and security institutions, which made their implementation difficult. This meeting, on the other hand, demonstrates that, across different centers of power, Iran’s political and military establishment is serious about diplomacy.

The seniority of the Iranians’ interlocutors also underscores the importance of these talks. Pakistan was represented by Field Marshal Asim Munir, the country’s de facto most influential political figure. Saudi Arabia sent Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, the younger brother and confidant of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, while Turkey sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, a longtime close advisor to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan with extensive experience in regional diplomacy.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan are also members of the Mecca defense pact, suggesting that Iran wants to play a greater role in the regional security architecture rather than acting outside of it. This is important, as Saudi Arabia in particular faces both continued attacks from Iran’s Houthi allies and risks becoming the target of IRGC strikes should the war break out again.

The meeting ended with a joint statement signed by Rezaei, Salman, Munir, and Kalin in which the four committed their countries to continued dialogue and regional “peace and security.” The statement was vague but signals that Iran does not want to immediately escalate and is instead open to having a productive relationship with its neighbors, some of whom it was targeting with missile and drone strikes just months earlier. This is supported by reports that the Iranian leadership responded positively to a letter sent last month by U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance to Rezaei, in which the former stressed the need for diplomacy.

But the meeting came on the heels of another significant development in the Iranian security landscape that signals that Iran is preparing to escalate if it must: the appointment of Mehrdad Akhlaghi as defense minister. His appointment indicates a shift in the defense establishment to a focus on offensive capabilities. Akhlaghi previously led the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group (SBIG), where he worked on developing Iran’s ballistic missiles, particularly those that use solid-fuel propellants. Compared to liquid-fuel missiles, solid-fuel missiles are easier to store, require less maintenance, and are less vulnerable to detection. As much of the U.S.-Israel strategy during the war centered on neutralizing Iran’s missiles, the importance of these operationally advantageous missiles should war break out again will increase—a consideration that may have played a role in Akhlaghi’s appointment.

After the SBIG, Akhlaghi went up the Iranian military-industrial ladder. He led the Aerospace Industries Organization, which oversees the missile program as a whole. He then headed the Defense Industries Organization, which oversees the manufacturing of all Iranian military hardware, including drones, which were also key to Iran’s military operations in the Gulf during this year’s war. His appointment marks a shift from his predecessor, Aziz Nasirzadeh, who was a former fighter pilot and came from Iran’s conventional air force, rather than institutions associated with the IRGC and its weaponry. Nasirzadeh was killed during the Feb. 28 attacks and, since then, the defense ministry had been led in the interim by Majid Ebn-e-Reza.

The U.S. military faces “profound” long-term readiness concerns, one expert said.

Akhlaghi will be tasked with rapidly rebuilding Iranian military capabilities—mainly missiles and drones—that have been degraded by U.S. and Israeli attacks. This suggests that Iran is preparing, simply put, to pummel the Gulf countries if war breaks out again.

In a recent speech, Akhlaghi stated that “if [U.S. President Donald] Trump drops a single bomb, his forces are going to leave the region horizontally (i.e., in body bags).” That would require a significant campaign against the Gulf—precisely the type of escalation that Salman was likely seeking to prevent during his time in Tehran. Akhlaghi’s influence in Iran could extend beyond the defense ministry to the SNSC, where he can participate in deliberations and vote on matters concerning national defense.

An insistence on regional diplomacy while simultaneously appointing a defense minister whose primary responsibility revolves around rebuilding the capabilities designed to wreak havoc on the Gulf might seem contradictory. But these moves reveal Iran’s broader strategy of hedging, at the core of which is a simple reality: Iran does not seem to know what is coming next.

In this state of limbo, Iran is watching international developments for clues as to what may be in store. Israeli elections, for example, have been covered extensively in Iranian media. Conservative outlets close to the supreme leader’s office, for instance, have amplified reports that Gadi Eisenkot, unlike incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is against regime change operations in Iran, as he has recognized that the Islamic Republic cannot be overthrown militarily. Eisenkot does not fully oppose military operations but instead believes that, should Israel attack Iran, it should target specific installations, such as nuclear facilities, rather than launch an all-out war.

Such reporting shows that, before the election, there was some cautious optimism in Iranian political circles: An Eisenkot-led government would be less willing to restart the war against Iran and might revert to smaller-scale sabotage operations that were common before the wars. From Tehran’s point of view, a change in Israeli leadership could also reduce the likelihood of renewed U.S. intervention, given Iran’s belief that Israel dragged the U.S. into the war.

Though Likud emerged as the party with the most votes, Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, and Eisenkot has warned Netanyahu against conducting an attack in the absence of a majority—even going as far as to call on security officials to stand firm against the prime minister. Netanyahu will have a tough time forming a government, as he would need to coax members of Eisenkot’s bloc into defecting. But Eisenkot, whose party underperformed in the elections, will also not be able to form a government without the support of Arab parties, which he has previously expressed opposition to including in any coalition.

Iran is also watching the American midterm elections, which similarly provoke more questions than answers. Some Iranian media sources have relayed reports from U.S. outlets that a Democratic victory in the midterms could constrain Trump’s ability to sustain a prolonged military campaign against Iran. Yet even if Democrats win control of Congress, they will not take office until January, leaving Trump two months to act without facing the constraints of a Democrat-controlled legislature. Once his party is freed from electoral pressures and concerns over rising gas prices, he might capitalize on that window to resume military action—even as his vice president is attempting to pursue diplomacy.

This uncertainty lies at the heart of Iran’s strategic calculations. Iran wants to convince its neighbors that it can be a partner for peace, while rebuilding its capacity to wage war. Whether diplomacy succeeds—or even has a chance to succeed—will depend on several factors, including who comes to power in Israel and how Trump acts after the midterms. In the meantime, Tehran is hoping for the best but expecting the worst.

Ashkan Hashemipour is a D.Phil. candidate at the University of Oxford in modern Iranian history and politics.

#6078. Senate Democrats claim early wins in trio of key states

Senate Democrats scored a few early wins in key races Tuesday night, according to The Associated Press, flipping the open seat in North Carolina and winning critical races in Georgia and New Hampshire.

Democrat Roy Cooper, the Tar Heel State’s battle-tested former governor who has never lost an election, extended his streak Tuesday by defeating Republican Michael Whatley. He becomes the first Democrat to win a Senate election in North Carolina since 2008.

In Georgia, Sen. Jon Ossoff, who started the midterm cycle as the most vulnerable Democratic senator, concluded it with a thrashing of his Republican opponent, Rep. Mike Collins.

And in New Hampshire, Rep. Chris Pappas will succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen after beating back a comeback attempt from Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu and denying Republicans one of their best pickup opportunities.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip the Senate, and polls heading into Election Day showed the party competitive in several Senate races in traditionally Republican turf.

With his victory Tuesday, Ossoff heads into his second term with a growing national profile powered by clips of his searing critiques of President Donald Trump.

The Democrat raised an eye-popping $136.6 million through Oct. 14, swamping Collins, who brought in $10.7 million.

Georgia is a swing state that Trump carried by about 2 points in 2024. Four years earlier, Joe Biden had won the state by less than a quarter of a percentage point.

Before taking on Ossoff, Collins had to contend with a multicandidate primary, including fellow Rep. Earl L. “Buddy” Carter and former football coach and first-time candidate Derek Dooley.

Collins picked up Trump’s endorsement before the June primary runoff with Dooley, but a recent Atlanta Journal-Constitution/University of Georgia poll found the president with a 55 percent job disapproval rating.

Collins had been dogged by a House Ethics inquiry and reports that his son-in-law shared antisemitic and white nationalist social media posts.

Senate Republicans had initially hoped to persuade Brian Kemp, the state’s popular governor, to run for the seat, but he opted to endorse Dooley instead.

Cooper’s decisive win over Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee, is a political blow to Trump, who was heavily invested in the contest.

The president publicly urged Whatley to run after Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, a sometimes critic, announced his retirement last year. Trump visited North Carolina twice since Labor Day, holding rallies in Gastonia and Greenville to boost Whatley. And Vice President JD Vance also campaigned for Whatley and other Republicans.

But Trump, who carried North Carolina in all three of his presidential races, has seen his approval fall sharply in the Tar Heel State: A poll released Sunday by the Center for Survey Research at East Carolina University found 54 percent of voters disapproving of the president’s performance.

At the start of the cycle, the North Carolina Senate race was thought to be among the nation’s most competitive. But on the eve of the election, Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rated the race Lean Democratic.

Senate Democrats had long been eager to recruit Cooper, who won four previous statewide elections for state attorney general and two as governor. He launched his campaign in July 2025, shortly after Tillis announced his retirement, and his fundraising prowess and deep roots in the state proved too much for Whatley, a first-time candidate, to overcome.

Cooper was also able to withstand GOP attacks that sought to paint him as a soft-on-crime ideologue who embraced a radical, far-left agenda and promoted “transgender ideology.”

Instead of diving into divisive culture war issues, Cooper hewed closely to an economic message, which was summed up by his campaign slogan: “Make Stuff Cost Less.” He portrayed Whately as a rubber-stamp for the unpopular president and a former energy company lobbyist who grew wealthy while rates rose.

The Trump administration “promised that cost of living would be the Day One issue,” Cooper said at a campaign stop in Rocky Mount last month. “Not only has that not been the case, they have made it so much worse.”

Pappas’ victory makes him the first openly gay man elected to the Senate, although he didn’t emphasize the potential milestone on the campaign trail.

A fourth-term House member, Pappas’ family owns a popular restaurant in the state that claims to have invented the chicken tender. He cast his campaign as crucial for Democrats to hold the Senate.

With his win, Pappas also dealt a loss to one of the state’s most prominent political families. Sununu’s father and brother previously served as New Hampshire governor.

Sununu, who conceded before 8:30 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday before the AP had called the race, was trying to win back a seat he held for a single term before losing to Shaheen in 2008.

The Granite State hasn’t elected a GOP senator since 2010, but Republicans, including Sununu’s brother, Chris, have been elected to the governor’s mansion every two years since 2016.

#6077. Can Washington Afford to Deter Chinese Cyber Activity?

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: Can Washington Afford to Deter Chinese Cyber Activity?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

In August, the U.S. Justice Department and the FBI dismantled the online infrastructure behind two hacking platforms operated by a Chinese state-sponsored group. It had been targeting sensitive U.S. government networks since at least 2018. In October, the agencies seized hacking tools used by another such group whose operations the U.S. government had previously disrupted in 2024.

Washington can deny Beijing’s hackers access to harmful capabilities. But the longevity and resurgence of the hackers’ campaigns raise a hard truth: Disruption alone cannot reverse the strategic advantages generated by years of Chinese cyber activity.

In August, the U.S. Justice Department and the FBI dismantled the online infrastructure behind two hacking platforms operated by a Chinese state-sponsored group. It had been targeting sensitive U.S. government networks since at least 2018. In October, the agencies seized hacking tools used by another such group whose operations the U.S. government had previously disrupted in 2024.

Washington can deny Beijing’s hackers access to harmful capabilities. But the longevity and resurgence of the hackers’ campaigns raise a hard truth: Disruption alone cannot reverse the strategic advantages generated by years of Chinese cyber activity.

The conventional U.S. approach to cyber deterrence has treated Chinese operations as individual security incidents. But to deter China from accruing advantages through cyber activity, the United States must change the incentives of a vast hacking ecosystem built around the Chinese state in order to counteract its impacts on the United States’ military, technology, and trade.

A shift is now underway in Washington. In March, the U.S. government’s 2026 Cyber Strategy promised sustained and aggressive action through public-private partnerships, which would combine offensive and defensive capabilities with economic and legal countermeasures. Recent reports from the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) and Britain’s Royal United Services Institute similarly advocate for coordinating cyber operations with other instruments of state power.

Such proposals appear to recognize that disrupting individual operations has not changed China’s broader cyber behavior. But while combining instruments may help disrupt individual operations and parts of the ecosystem, they may still fail to credibly deter the broader pattern of activity that generates cumulative advantage.

Therein lies the more troubling possibility: that the United States cannot credibly deter the broad pattern of Chinese cyber activity at a price that it is prepared—or willing—to sustain.

China’s recent cyber campaigns have advantages beyond individual intrusions. In 2023, for example, the Volt Typhoon campaign secured access to U.S. infrastructure in Guam that would be critical for U.S. operations in a future Taiwan contingency. While the United States removed some of the original footholds, the Justice Department has warned that the target infrastructure is still vulnerable; in early 2025, security analysts found that a Volt Typhoon-linked group had steadily penetrated U.S. utilities through that year. Disrupting individual intrusions had not prevented China from prepositioning for future disruption.

The year after the Guam intrusion, a campaign attributed to the Salt Typhoon hacker network compromised U.S. telecommunications networks, allowing Chinese actors to collect sensitive information from surveillance systems. More than a year after the intrusion was first disclosed, the campaign was discovered to be surveilling congressional staffers’ communications. It is still unclear whether Salt Typhoon infrastructure has been removed from the affected networks or whether it continues to accumulate intelligence.

A broad campaign of deterrence has proved to be largely ineffective, but it was once possible to think in narrower terms. In 2015, then-U.S. President Barack Obama and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed that neither side would conduct or knowingly support cyber-enabled theft of intellectual property for commercial advantage. Security firms subsequently reported a decline in detected Chinese intrusions against U.S. companies (although the decline had begun before the agreement, and its causes remain contested).

The agreement did not end Chinese cyber espionage. It did, however, identify a relatively narrow category of conduct—commercial theft—that the two governments could explicitly agree to restrain, as opposed to the broader range of purposes that Chinese cyber operations now serve, from espionage to conflict prepositioning.

Washington no longer faces a discrete category of conduct around which to organize a deterrence effort. Today, it must determine which activities deserve a response, how much future risk they pose, and what consequences might discourage further operations. A response calibrated to an intrusion’s immediate effects may miss its future significance. Punishing every instance of access that might someday be used disruptively, meanwhile, would be difficult to sustain.

Similarly, punishing any single actor or intermediary that enables Chinese cyber operations is no longer enough to deter the wider ecosystem. Contractors disappear and reemerge frequently. The company disrupted in October provided hacking services to the People’s Liberation Army and the Ministry of State Security (MSS); others have conducted intrusions for both the MSS and the Ministry of Public Security. Rather than relying on single, self-contained operations, Chinese security organizations draw on overlapping external providers, creating an ecosystem that can regenerate operational capacity even amid disruptions.

Washington thinks offensive cyber power will restore deterrence. It’s mistaken.

Allies fear that Washington is retreating from leadership at the worst possible time.

For Washington, sanctions, export restrictions, criminal investigations, and public exposure could threaten the commercial interests and personal security of these actors. Rewards and protections encouraging people inside the enabling network to disclose information or defect, as proposed by the CFR report, could change incentives within the ecosystem, not merely punish its visible members. Pressure could make providers more cautious, expose links between companies and state agencies, and make operations harder to mount. At the state level, a credible threat of coordinated economic and diplomatic consequences might also discourage activities that Beijing considers too costly.

Yet such proposals contain significant shortcomings. Many enablers operate inside China, where they have little exposure to U.S. markets or financial systems, and their main sources of income come from state customers. In the past, sanctions have dismantled individual companies fronting the state. They would continue to have little lasting effect on companies that are dependent on Chinese security agencies, since Beijing can fund, protect, or replace providers when their work serves a strategic purpose.

Crucially, imposing costs on a contractor changes Beijing’s calculation only if the contractor’s financial, operational, or reputational losses degrade a longer-term strategic capability, threatens to expose other state-sponsored operations, or makes replacement offensive capabilities more costly for the wider ecosystem. If a state agency can absorb the loss and find another supplier, then Washington will have spent resources on punishing a node without changing the demand for its services. Previous attempts to identify and disrupt such valuable nodes have simply resulted in a temporary lull before resurgence.

To put meaningful pressure on Beijing, Washington would need to credibly signal that specific Chinese cyber activities would trigger costs substantial enough to change Chinese leaders’ calculations. That would require coordinated measures in more visible areas of strategic competition, such as restrictions on semiconductor exports or access to U.S. markets.

But China could retaliate in areas of competition where it retains leverage, such as by further restricting U.S. access to rare earth and critical mineral supplies, disrupting U.S. defense production. In that case, efforts to protect national security by deterring Chinese cyber activity could ultimately undermine it elsewhere.

Washington would thus need to accept immediate economic costs in return for uncertain deterrent effects for as long as necessary, when even sustained pressure may not stop the wider accumulation of access and intelligence. For the United States, China’s cyber operations may simply not hold enough strategic or political significance to warrant that economic price.

That leaves Washington with a dilemma. When espionage today can become disruption tomorrow, the value of deterring a wider range of cyber activity must be weighed against the costs of sustaining those restrictions and absorbing countermeasures. The challenge is to cast a wide enough net to address the sources of future risk while keeping threats specific and credible enough to influence behavior.

Accepting these risks does not have to mean abandoning deterrence; Washington can still seek to prevent China from using its access to U.S. infrastructure to disrupt essential services or pressure U.S. leaders during a crisis. But it should not confuse deterring a specific act with deterring the wider pattern of activity that accumulates strategic advantages over time.

Access may be the most valuable when it remains concealed, preserving China’s choice of whether and when to leverage it and leaving Washington to bear the costs of preparing for multiple possible outcomes. The more that Beijing believes Washington will tolerate continued accumulation, the greater its incentive to preserve that position and scale it—as the price for the United States only grows higher with time.

Ahana Datta Fasel is the author of Full Stack Spies: Cyber Espionage in the Age of US-China Competition (Hurst). She advises U.K. Research and Innovation on national security and defense.

#6074. Brazil’s Economic Impasse

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MONICA DE BOLLE is Senior Fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, an Adjunct Professor at Georgetown University, and a co-author of The New Economic Nationalism.

Neither Lula nor Bolsonaro Can Solve the Country’s Problems

On October 5, the day after the first round of Brazil’s general elections, the country’s financial markets were euphoric. Brazil is struggling with high debt and low growth, and investors are eager for leaders to reduce budget deficits, deregulate, cut taxes, and perhaps even privatize state assets. After nearly four years under the left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, who has been slow to implement such measures, investors hope a right-wing government will create opportunities for bold reform.

Rule by the right might be exactly what Brazil gets. The far-right Liberal Party made substantial gains in the legislature, becoming the single largest party in both the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. Its presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the notorious former President Jair Bolsonaro, led the aging incumbent, Lula, by nearly two percentage points in the first round of voting. Lula has shown himself capable of impressive political comebacks, but Flávio Bolsonaro is still the favorite in the runoff vote scheduled for October 25.

Even if Bolsonaro wins, however, the prospects for the Brazilian economy are dim. The policies he has put forward are nothing close to the substantial fiscal consolidation program that will be necessary to bring down debt and stimulate private investment, and his determination to weaken Brazil’s political institutions creates the kind of uncertainty that scares investors away. Economic growth has been sluggish under Lula, whose administration has struggled to relieve the high debt burdens afflicting the public sector and households. What would truly doom the country to economic crisis, however, is the kind of authoritarian-inspired politics that a Bolsonaro government could usher in.

Brazil is in serious economic trouble. The country’s sovereign debt ratio has ballooned to 83 percent of GDP, fiscal deficits leave no room for additional government spending, and high interest rates are hurting consumers and investors. Meanwhile, the Iran war has raised the price of fuel and other goods, weighing on household balance sheets already strained by high debt and leaving many Brazilians desperate for leaders who can alleviate their daily hardships.

This predicament is years in the making. Before Jair Bolsonaro was elected in 2018, his predecessor, President Michel Temer, enacted a cap on public spending to contain Brazil’s runaway fiscal problems. Temer introduced the cap as a constitutional amendment to prevent future governments from changing the spending ceiling to suit their needs. Yet Jair Bolsonaro raised the cap several times anyway, which required convincing Congress to amend the constitution. In return, the executive branch effectively ceded control of the budgetary process to the legislature.

Lula therefore inherited a system in which he had little room for fiscal adjustment, and he made few attempts to fix the problem during his term. The result was high budget deficits and persistent inflation, which forced the central bank to raise interest rates substantially. In turn, high interest rates damaged household balance sheets and lowered overall investment and growth.

If Lula were reelected, he would find it incredibly difficult to introduce new fiscal reforms and other measures to support growth. He promised to reduce spending and has proposed a comprehensive overhaul of Brazil’s tax system, which would help increase the budget surplus and reduce public debt. Yet Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies now hold a majority of seats in the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies, allowing them to block any legislation Lula might pursue.

Yet it is overly optimistic, if not completely unrealistic, to expect that Bolsonaro would fare better. Neither candidate has provided much detail during the campaign about what he would do to fix the economy. Bolsonaro has instead spoken often about “institutional reforms,” which he has said would include amending Brazil’s 38-year-old constitution to make existing labor and environmental regulations more flexible, among other changes; meddling with the Supreme Court; and granting amnesty to his father, who is serving a prison sentence for leading a 2023 coup attempt. Those steps are likely to drive away investors because stable institutions are necessary for an economy to function well. A government that undermines the judicial system and the constitution will compromise the integrity of its economic policies, no matter what those policies are or how good the reputations of the officials making them may be.

Gathering support for such an overhaul of the country’s political institutions, moreover, would require compromises that could worsen Brazil’s economic troubles. To secure enough votes in Congress to advance Bolsonaro’s priorities—for example, two-thirds of the Senate would need to approve the removal of a Supreme Court justice, and three-fifths of both houses must approve a constitutional amendment—the government would have to bring legislators outside its coalition on board. Those politicians would almost certainly demand substantial funds for their constituencies in exchange for their support, adding to the budget deficit.

Bolsonaro’s far-right movement will also be focused on holding together its recently formed coalition of governors, mayors, and voters. Much of its constituency is lower-middle-class Brazilians who rose out of poverty during the boom years two decades ago, while Lula was serving his first two terms in office. After seeing their income growth stagnate in the years since, these voters have turned to the Liberal Party, but their loyalty is new. Most are self-employed and face economic precarity. Both Bolsonaro and Lula are now trying to appeal to these voters by promising initiatives that boost income and offer household debt relief, but delivering such programs—if it is even possible—would only exacerbate Brazil’s economic woes.

What Bolsonaro has shared about his economic policies does not inspire much confidence, either. His party has said it would reduce government spending by $40 billion, or 1.5 percent of GDP, and deliver primary budget surpluses—a measure of the budget balance that does not include interest payments. But it has not explained how it would accomplish this, nor has Bolsonaro elaborated on his vague plans for controlling the rise in public debt. Ultimately, it is unlikely that Bolsonaro can deliver on any of these promises, especially if he keeps his pledge not to cut pensions and key social programs.

Part of the problem is that the Liberal Party’s economic program lacks a viable plan for reducing costs. It proposes eliminating at least ten government ministries but has no estimate of the resulting cost savings. When Jair Bolsonaro took similar steps after he assumed office in 2019, removing cabinet positions and laying off public servants, those moves had little effect on fiscal outcomes. Other promised measures include reducing Brazil’s value-added tax, phasing out a tax on financial transactions, lowering taxes on electricity and fuel, spending $180 billion on infrastructure over four years, and building 2.5 million new homes. None of them would fix Brazil’s fiscal problems; they would only make those problems worse.

The same goes for the rest of Flávio Bolsonaro’s tax plan. His economic advisers have said they intend to reverse every tax created or raised under Lula’s finance minister, Fernando Haddad. Haddad’s tax increases were intended to shift the tax burden to high-income brackets, raise government revenue, and reduce inequalities in the tax system. These taxes have contributed to a modest increase in revenue but fell short of delivering budgetary surpluses. Bolsonaro has argued that the measures are impeding investment because they tax higher income brackets more heavily, but there is no evidence to support this idea. Instead, repealing all these tax increases would worsen Brazil’s fiscal situation. A simple calculation shows that Brazil needs to increase its primary budget balance by about six percent of GDP, either through increased revenue or decreased spending (or both), to keep its debt from rising further. That adjustment would have to be spread over at least three years, giving indebted households and firms time to change their consumption and investment patterns, to avoid a recession. Slashing taxes, however, would reduce government revenues, raising the debt.

Brazil’s high interest rates are another constraint. The central bank’s current rate is 13.75 percent, astronomical by Latin American standards, dictating interest rates everywhere in the economy. Public debt service payments alone consume some 8.7 percent of GDP. Bolsonaro would not be able to lower interest rates significantly without sparking a recession, so he would face the same problem that has plagued Lula during his latest term—few good options for containing a rapidly growing debt.

Neither Lula nor Bolsonaro is well positioned to solve Brazil’s economic problems. A decisive turn toward illiberalism under Bolsonaro, however, would all but assure economic disaster.

Flávio Bolsonaro has never disavowed his father’s championing of Brazil’s dictatorship, which lasted from 1964 to 1985, and his Liberal Party traces its lineage to the party that sustained the military regime. Moreover, he has pledged to release his father and his father’s associates who are in prison for staging an insurrection and a coup attempt in 2023. Flávio’s brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, a former member of Brazil’s Congress who would likely play a significant role in his brother’s government, has openly expressed his admiration for Viktor Orban’s illiberal regime in Hungary, claiming a desire to learn the “best practices” of a movement that rewrote Hungary’s constitution, reshaped its courts, silenced its press, and deployed other overtly authoritarian tactics. And the substantial far-right bloc in Brazil’s Congress supports policies to undermine institutions, including by impeaching members of the Supreme Court—a step these parties advocated even before corruption allegations emerged against several of the court’s justices. (Flávio Bolsonaro is also under investigation for his involvement in the same corruption scandal.)

Although Brazil is not at risk of returning to military rule, the former authoritarian regime serves as a warning of what could happen if a Bolsonaro administration follows its illiberal inclinations to their logical conclusion. During those two decades of military dictatorship, Brazil spent at unsustainable levels, mostly funding state enterprises, to preserve the regime’s hold on power. The country defaulted on its public debt, endured corrosive hyperinflation, and saw income inequality skyrocket. Six economic stabilization plans failed and growth stagnated. Brazil is not alone in this experience. No Latin American country that swung from democracy to authoritarian rule in the past century has benefited economically from the shift. Countries elsewhere in the world that prospered after such a transition, including some in East Asia, became less authoritarian during their economic ascent.

Brazil’s rightward shift fits a regional pattern. The common thread that unites Brazil with Argentina, Chile, and Colombia is the crude libertarian worldview that each of their far-right movements espouse. All of them talk about citizens becoming entrepreneurs free of the state. They tell voters who have unstable employment and little economic security that their policies will bring prosperity. But their populism rarely wins the confidence of investors. Like its peers, when the Brazilian far right says it can overcome the country’s substantial problems with institutional demolition and a threadbare economic agenda, what it really offers is empty promises.

#6072. Why Kushner and Witkoff Keep Failing

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Why Kushner and Witkoff Keep Failing

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are unofficial presidential envoys, personally selected by U.S. President Donald Trump to handle critical negotiations over Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran. While it’s safe to say neither was selected after a long and extensive search (Kushner is Trump’s son-in-law and Witkoff is a longtime friend and golfing buddy), let’s be charitable and assume that they have been genuinely trying to reach agreements that would advance U.S. interests. The question is: Why have they accomplished so little?

Look at the record: The supposed peace deal over Gaza is a sham, as Israel continues to bomb Gaza with impunity, expand its territorial control there, and limit relief aid while tolerating (if not actively helping) Israeli settlers’ violent campaign against Palestinians in the West Bank. Genuine peace may not have been their real objective, however, as Kushner and Witkoff are both ardent Israel supporters who were even less likely to put serious pressure on Israel than former U.S. President Joe Biden (which is saying something). In this view, the Gaza agreement was a Potemkin peace deal whose main goal was to free Israeli hostages held by Hamas and get the conflict off the front pages while tying Israel’s hands as little as possible. If so, then one might concede that they accomplished their objective. But if the goal was peace, they failed.

Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are unofficial presidential envoys, personally selected by U.S. President Donald Trump to handle critical negotiations over Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran. While it’s safe to say neither was selected after a long and extensive search (Kushner is Trump’s son-in-law and Witkoff is a longtime friend and golfing buddy), let’s be charitable and assume that they have been genuinely trying to reach agreements that would advance U.S. interests. The question is: Why have they accomplished so little?

Look at the record: The supposed peace deal over Gaza is a sham, as Israel continues to bomb Gaza with impunity, expand its territorial control there, and limit relief aid while tolerating (if not actively helping) Israeli settlers’ violent campaign against Palestinians in the West Bank. Genuine peace may not have been their real objective, however, as Kushner and Witkoff are both ardent Israel supporters who were even less likely to put serious pressure on Israel than former U.S. President Joe Biden (which is saying something). In this view, the Gaza agreement was a Potemkin peace deal whose main goal was to free Israeli hostages held by Hamas and get the conflict off the front pages while tying Israel’s hands as little as possible. If so, then one might concede that they accomplished their objective. But if the goal was peace, they failed.

Similarly, their efforts to negotiate an agreement with Iran before the war never went anywhere, in part because these two amateur diplomats apparently didn’t understand some critical technical details regarding Iran’s nuclear program but also because Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu decided to launch a war while talks were underway. As with Gaza, the negotiations may have been something of a sham from the start, intended not to reach a lasting agreement but to allow time to prepare for another round of war.

Russia’s war in Ukraine is still raging, too—a direct refutation of Trump’s campaign boast that he could end it in 24 hours. Witkoff and Kushner have met with Russian officials on multiple occasions and offered increasingly generous inducements, even as the administration keeps pressuring Kyiv to cut a deal. The result has been not peace but more war, including expanding attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine and Russia alike.

If judged by whether their efforts have led to peace, in short, Kushner and Witkoff are 0 for 3. To be fair, handling all three of these conflicts at once would tax the abilities of an Otto von Bismarck or a Henry Kissinger, and trying to conduct complex and difficult diplomacy on behalf of an erratic president who is more interested in appearances than achievements would be a challenge for any negotiator. But these handicaps don’t fully explain their repeated failures.

Trump’s son-in-law embodies the rise of a trend that threatens to ignite a new nuclear age.

One can think of several reasons why their efforts have been unsuccessful, but a big part of the problem is their overarching worldview. Kushner and Witkoff and Trump are all real estate developers who are preoccupied with making money. That’s the only thing that really matters to them, which is why Trump seems more interested in monetizing the presidency than he is in actually governing and why Kushner may have pocketed billions of dollars in secret payments from the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia (an accusation he denies). If you assume that everyone else is also on the make, then the way to get to yes is to offer your counterparts a sweet deal that will make them richer. In this world, everyone has their price, and the trick is to figure out what that price is and then convince them you can meet it.

This one-dimensional perspective was already evident in Trump’s first term. It lay behind Kushner’s belief that the key to Middle East peace was to ignore the Palestinian desire for statehood or political rights and focus instead on promoting business deals among Israel, some wealthy Gulf states, and (eventually) Saudi Arabia. That same instinct underlay Trump’s belief that he could get North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to give up his arsenal of nuclear weapons by offering an alluring vision of ritzy resorts and luxury condos along North Korean beaches, an idea later recycled as a potential blueprint for Gaza. And it is obviously central to recent attempts to persuade the Kremlin to end its war in Ukraine by buying some Russian diesel fuel, letting Russian companies help develop gas fields in Alaska, talking up lucrative future business deals, and ending Moscow’s economic isolation from the West.

The obvious flaw in this worldview is its failure to recognize that the top priority for smart political leaders isn’t money or wealth—it’s national security. Security is more important because without it, one’s wealth is vulnerable: Having all the money in the world is useless if someone stronger can take it from you. Look at what happened to Kuwait in 1990, when Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein decided to invade the wealthy emirate, simultaneously eliminating one of his main creditors and gaining control of resources that would have increased Iraq’s GDP by roughly 40 percent. And his gambit would have worked had a coalition of outside powers not ridden to Kuwait’s rescue.

Wealth is far from irrelevant, of course, and greed can be a powerful motivator, too. I don’t doubt that Russian President Vladimir Putin would be happy to pocket all those blandishments that Kushner and Witkoff keep dangling as part of an eventual peace deal in Ukraine. But if all he cared about were money, he wouldn’t have invaded Ukraine in the first place, and he wouldn’t have continued to wage war there at considerable economic and human cost. Unless and until the security concerns (whether exaggerated or not) that drove his decision to invade are met, offering him a bunch of economic goodies isn’t going to end the war.

The same is true for Kyiv, of course: If money were all that mattered, the smart move would be to accept the loss of Crimea and the Donbas and hold out for a big aid package to rebuild Ukraine’s shattered economy. But Ukrainians don’t want to surrender lands they regard as rightly theirs, even for a price. Equally important, they don’t want to live in fear of future Russian threats. Thus, a future peace arrangement would have to meet both sides’ security concerns as well as their economic desires.

Nations also care about preserving their identity and cultural autonomy, and those living under a foreign yoke often want to govern themselves. As a result, these groups will sometimes make enormous sacrifices to try to establish their own state. Palestinians won’t abandon their national identity or desire for political rights in exchange for a lucrative economic package (even assuming one were genuinely on offer), and neither will any number of other aspiring national movements. That same sense of national pride also helps explain why bombing other countries to topple a regime or get it to surrender rarely works, even when it is coupled with the prospect of future economic benefits. On the contrary, such actions tend to rally the population behind leaders who might otherwise lack broad support and make them even less willing to compromise.

International politics, in short, is not like real estate development because relations among states take place in an arena where there is no central authority and where some states have the ability and the will to use violence to get what they want. In such a world, states have powerful incentives to guarantee their own security first and then worry about how to become more prosperous. A solid grasp of how business works and experience negotiating complicated deals can be an asset in diplomacy (as former Secretaries of State George Shultz and James Baker demonstrated)—but only if you understand the critical differences between these two realms. Regrettably, Kushner and Witkoff (and Trump) show no sign of having understood the distinction or of having learned very much from their experiences to date. But they (or their families) are making some serious bank while these conflicts rage on, which may have been the real goal all along.

Stephen M. Walt is a columnist at Foreign Policy and the Robert and Renée Belfer professor of international relations at Harvard University. Walt is the author of The New Geopolitics, a five-part newsletter masterclass breaking down the biggest concepts you should use to navigate today’s world. #6070. Longtime Dem Sen who lost his seat 2 years ago projected to secure comeback victory in midterm battleground

Vivek Ramaswamy addressed supporters at GOP headquarters in Columbus after the gubernatorial race was called for Democrat Amy Acton.

Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is projected to win his bid to return to the U.S. Senate, defeating Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio just two years after losing his seat to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, the Fox News Decision Desk projects.

Brown’s victory marks a remarkable political comeback for the longtime Ohio Democrat, who served in the Senate from 2007 until 2025 before Moreno ousted him in one of the most closely watched races of the 2024 election.

The Democrat will return to Washington after defeating Husted in a special election to serve the remainder of the term originally won by Vice President JD Vance. Husted was appointed to the seat by Republican Gov. Mike DeWine in January 2025 after Vance resigned from the Senate to serve as President Donald Trump's No. 2.

Brown previously represented Ohio in the U.S. House and served as the state’s secretary of state and a member of the Ohio House.

THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND

Sen. Jon Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown will face off in a highly anticipated Senate race in Ohio in November. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images ; Justin Merriman/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The timing of Brown’s return to Washington will depend on when Ohio certifies the election and when he is formally sworn in. Brown could be sworn in during the lame-duck session, potentially changing the Senate’s voting math before the new Congress convenes.

The Ohio race was viewed as a key battleground because Democrats saw the state as one of their best opportunities to erode the GOP’s narrow Senate majority, while Republicans viewed Husted’s seat as critical to maintaining control of the chamber.

FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Sherrod Brown speaks with reporters after casting his ballot at the Franklin County Board of Elections on Oct. 6, 2026 in Columbus, Ohio. (Jeff Dean/Getty Images)

Brown’s win came two years after he lost his Senate seat to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, as Ohio continued its shift toward the GOP in presidential elections. Former President Donald Trump carried the state by 11 percentage points in 2024, and Republicans argued that Brown’s return would amount to a restoration of the Democratic establishment that Ohio voters had rejected.

Brown sought to overcome those headwinds by emphasizing his record on manufacturing, organized labor, trade, consumer protections and economic issues. His campaign focused heavily on the cost of living, gas and diesel prices, health care and the impact of Republican policies on working-class Ohioans.

The candidates also clashed over data centers and energy costs. Brown criticized Husted’s role in supporting major economic development projects involving data centers, arguing that Ohio taxpayers and consumers could be left responsible for the infrastructure and energy demands associated with the facilities.

Ohio Sen. Jon Husted revealed on Monday that a record 75 sheriffs in the state have endorsed him, including independents and a Democrat. (Husted Senate campaign)

Husted defended the projects as a way to bring jobs and investment to Ohio. He also pointed to legislation aimed at preventing taxpayers from bearing the operating costs of large data centers which Democrats blocked in the Senate.

Husted, a longtime figure in Ohio Republican politics, campaigned on his record as the state’s lieutenant governor, secretary of state and House speaker. He argued that Brown would return to Washington as a reliable vote for Senate Democrats and national party leaders.

Brown's victory gives Democrats a huge boost in their bid to take back control of the United States Senate when the votes are all counted after Election Day.
